chunks.text: TL;DR
Every restaurant ends up needing the same dozen image sizes across G B P, Yelp, your site, social, OG, and menu thumbnails.
Shoot once at 30% above the recommended resolution. You can crop down; you cannot crop up.
A consistent angle on menu thumbnails matters more than camera quality. Mixed angles make the menu page read as broken.
Re-shoot twice a year. Photo cadence is one of the few maintenance loops that visibly affects average review rating.

Every restaurant ends up needing the same dozen image sizes, but almost no one shoots them at once. The result: a Google Business Profile cover that is the wrong aspect ratio and got cropped weirdly, a Yelp photo that is portrait when Yelp wants landscape, a menu page where every dish photo is a different shape and the layout breaks.
This is the spec sheet I send every studio client and every photographer I work with. One shoot, the right specs in advance, and the result drops cleanly into every surface.
The 10 image sizes you actually need.

One shoot, ten outputs · the resolution rule. Shoot once, at 30% above max: You can always crop down. You can never crop up. (source). Site surfaces: Hero, interior banners, menu thumbnails, OG/Twitter card. (derivatives). G B P surfaces: Cover photo, profile, gallery — three different aspects. (derivatives). Social + Yelp: Yelp cover, Instagram square, Instagram portrait. (derivatives). One shoot, ten outputs · the resolution rule.
Resolution rules.

Always shoot at the resolution recommended above PLUS roughly 30% extra. You can always crop down; you can never crop up. A hero shot at 2400 times 1024 lets you also produce the 1200 times 630 OG card from the same file; a hero shot at 1200 times 630 leaves you stuck.
For images that ship to your site, export as C D N -friendly WebP at 80% quality — it is typically 60-70% smaller than JPG without visible loss.
Alt text — the most-skipped part of the spec sheet.

Every image needs alt text . Not "IMG_4521.jpg," not the menu name, not "delicious food." A specific descriptive sentence: "Plate of carnitas with cilantro, white onion, and lime on a wood board." Costs 5 seconds per photo and earns you S E O + accessibility + AI-search citation.
For a 30-photo restaurant shoot, that is 150 seconds — or two minutes — of writing. Skip it and you have left every photo's S E O value on the floor.
The shot list to hand a photographer.

Run Photo Brief . It generates a per-surface shot list with the spec sheet attached — exactly the document you would hand a photographer the morning of the shoot. Save the brief to your Workshop so you can re-run it for the next seasonal shoot.

The shoot itself is usually 2-3 hours for a 30-photo deliverable: the hero, 10-15 dishes, 4-6 room shots, 2-3 detail shots (a hand pouring wine, smoke off a grill, the chef plating). Done in one go, you have material for every surface for the next 12 months.
The "shoot it yourself with a phone" version.

If hiring a photographer is not in budget, the phone version still works. Modern phones in good light routinely beat low-effort DSLR work — the variable that matters most is not the sensor, it is the time of day and the angle to the window. Three rules:
Daylight only. Shoot 11 AM to 2 PM near a window. Restaurant overhead lighting reads orange and dingy on the phone sensor.
One angle per dish, repeated. Pick top-down OR 3/4 front, and use the same angle for every dish so the menu page reads as one set.
Edit lightly. Increase exposure +0.3, boost shadows. Skip filters.

Shoot cadence · twice a year + menu changes. Pre-summer shoot: Memorial Day prep — patio, lighter dishes, daylight cocktails. (core set). Pre-holiday shoot: Mid-October prep — fall menu, warm tones, room shots. (core set). Menu pivot shoot: Any major menu change — new dishes, removed dishes, season swaps. (as needed). Shoot cadence · twice a year + menu changes.
How often to re-shoot.

Twice a year. Once before peak season (Memorial Day for summer, mid-October for the holidays); once when the menu changes substantially. If you re-shoot less than once a year, the photos start looking dated to regulars even if they are still technically accurate.

Save the dates in your Workshop alongside your Margin Math and Restaurant Audit scenarios. The compounding argument: photo cadence is one of the few maintenance loops that visibly affects average review rating, because the G B P cover and the menu thumbnails set the expectation guests bring through the door — and reviews are written against that expectation, not against the food alone.
Bad photos do not just fail to help. They actively drag the average down by setting the wrong expectation before anyone walks in the door.
Key takeaways
10 sizes cover every surface you actually need. Hand the spec sheet to your photographer with the brief.
WebP at 80% quality cuts file size 60–70% vs JPG, no visible loss.
Alt text is the most-skipped 5 seconds per photo and the highest-leverage one for S E O + AI search.
The phone version works in good light — the variable that matters most is time of day, not the sensor.
Re-shoot dates: Memorial Day prep, mid-October prep, plus any major menu change.
Generate the shot list before the photographer arrives.

Photo Brief outputs a per-surface shot list with the spec sheet attached — exactly what you would hand a photographer the morning of the shoot. Saves to your Workshop so you can re-run for the next seasonal shoot.
